analysis.one_liner: Strips OSHA's power to issue emergency workplace safety rules and bans any federal requirement that workers get a vaccine.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a House vote and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the OSHA law so that the agency could no longer issue emergency temporary standards — the fast, short-term safety rules it can impose during a crisis like a pandemic — and would explicitly bar OSHA from ever requiring an employee to take a vaccine, drug, or other biological product. It was written in response to OSHA's COVID-19 vaccine-or-testing mandate. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers benefit most: they would face no risk of emergency OSHA safety mandates, including any future vaccine-or-testing requirement, and would keep full control over their own workplace health policies. Workers who oppose mandatory vaccination would gain the legal certainty that no federal workplace safety rule can require them to take one.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the statutory section that lets the Labor Secretary issue emergency temporary standards, so no future administration could impose an immediate workplace safety mandate while a permanent rule is being written.
It adds an explicit prohibition on OSHA requiring any employee to take a drug, vaccine, or other biological product, permanently closing the door on workplace vaccination requirements under OSHA.

analysis.who_pays: Workers pay, in the form of weaker protection during future emergencies: without emergency temporary standards, OSHA cannot respond quickly to a new pandemic or toxic exposure, and the ban on requiring any drug or vaccine limits the tools available to keep workers safe.

drawbacks.text: Repealing emergency temporary standards would remove the government's only tool for imposing immediate safety rules during a sudden crisis, such as a pandemic or a newly discovered chemical hazard, leaving workers unprotected until a slow permanent rule is finished.

The bill would bar OSHA not just from vaccine mandates but from any workplace rule requiring medical treatment, so a future outbreak could not be met with mandatory vaccination of front-line workers even where exposure risk is high.
The prohibition applies broadly to any drug or biological product, going beyond the COVID-19 controversy that prompted it and limiting future safety responses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives employers and workers clear notice that OSHA cannot impose emergency vaccine mandates, which supporters see as a bodily-autonomy safeguard. The cost is permanent: it strips the government's fastest tool for responding to urgent workplace hazards and bans safety rules covering medical treatments, leaving workers without federal protection if a future outbreak or toxic exposure demands a fast mandate. On balance the gains are narrow and the safety loss is broad.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 30, 2022, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
The only action after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on March 31, 2022; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who want no OSHA emergency mandates are better off; the bill's death also preserved OSHA's emergency safety authority.

for.name: Rep. Andrew Clyde
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 32 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 supporters (sponsor plus cosponsors) were Republicans, and the bill received no Democratic cosponsors.

industries.industry: Employers (especially large workplaces subject to OSHA rules)
industries.note: The bill removes the threat of emergency safety mandates, including the vaccine-or-testing requirement, and blocks any future medical-treatment rules, reducing compliance costs and giving employers final say over workplace health policies.
OSHA loses its emergency response authority, weakening the agency workers rely on for fast protection, though its permanent rulemaking authority is untouched.
